extracted.intended_audience: seminarians, Catholic theologians, clergy, and students of dogmatic theology
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the Catholic doctrine of sanctifying (justifying) grace: its nature, metaphysical status, relation to charity and the Holy Ghost, its effects, and its role as the formal cause of justification (as developed especially in the Council of Trent and Scholastic theology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctifying grace the sole formal cause of justification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Council of Trent defined that 'sanctifying grace of itself is able to produce all the formal effects of justification, e.g. forgiveness of sins, the sanctification of the sinner, his adoption by God,' and consequently requires no supplementary or contributory causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doctrine rejects views that would make justification depend on an 'imputed' or extraneous justice (e.g., Butzer's claim) or that intrinsic righteousness is inadequate without a 'favor Dei externus'. The Tridentine decision implies justification is wholly accomplished by the infusion of sanctifying grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incompatibility of sanctifying grace and sin
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctifying grace and sin cannot co-exist in the same subject; Scripture and Tradition present them as mutually exclusive (darkness vs. light, life vs. death).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text surveys theological positions about the nature of this opposition: (a) purely moral opposition (Nominalists/Scotists), (b) physical contrariety (Suarez and some Jesuits), and (c) metaphysical contradiction (Thomists and majority of Jesuits). The Thomist/metaphysical view best accords with Scripture though not declared theologically certain. Practical implications: if grace truly sanctifies, it must exclude mortal/original sin in the same subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctifying grace conceived as a permanent quality (qualitas permanens) of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctifying grace is to be conceived as an infused, inherent, permanent state in the soul—'the charity of God is poured forth by the Holy Spirit in the hearts of those that are justified, and is inherent therein.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments: Biblical language (new life, regeneration), the Council of Trent's wording ('infused' and 'inherent'), and the fact that infant baptism imparts the same kind of grace as adult baptism (so it cannot be merely transient actual graces). The Council declined an explicit metaphysical declaration but indicated permanence by 'inhaeret'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctifying grace as an infused habit (habitus infusus)
rubrics_metrics.description: While terminological difficulties exist, sanctifying grace may be described as an infused habit—a permanent quality which, though not a habit in the strict Aristotelian operative sense, corresponds to a 'habit' insofar as it is a stable principle of being in the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholastic distinctions: entitative vs. operative habit. Grace is primarily an entitative habit (a quality inhering in the soul's substance) but also imparts, by infusion, the power to perform supernatural acts and so has an operative aspect. Because the supernatural cannot be acquired by nature, such habits are necessarily infused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace is not identical with the Holy Ghost (gratia increata)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctifying grace is not the uncreated Person of the Holy Ghost; the Holy Ghost is the efficient cause who 'pours forth' grace, but grace itself is a created, infused quality in the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: If the Holy Ghost were identical with sanctifying grace, then statements that grace 'may be increased by good works' or that the Holy Ghost is 'poured forth in hearts' would imply pantheism. Thus theologians like St. Thomas and the Council of Trent reject identifying grace with the Person of the Holy Ghost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctifying grace as an accidental form (not a new substance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grace must be conceived as an accident—specifically a quality—that inheres in the soul, not as a created substance or substantial form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical argument: a thing that exists by inhering in another is an accident; sanctifying grace inheres in the soul's substance and so is an accidental form (qualitas). Medieval debates about whether grace is a created substance are rejected as contradictory; Thomists hold it is an accidental quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction (or identity) between sanctifying grace and charity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a debated question whether sanctifying grace is identical with the theological virtue of charity (love); some (Scotus, Bellarmine, Molina et al.) hold identity or virtual identity, while the majority (St. Thomas and his school) maintain a real distinction: grace as a habit of being, charity as an operative habit (virtue) residing in faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments for identity cite Scriptural interchangeability of effects and certain Patristic language. Arguments for distinction emphasize different metaphysical types (entitative vs. operative), the logical order (grace precedes charity), and conciliar/traditional distinctions. The Church has not rendered an official definitive decision; both positions explained with citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctifying grace as participation in the divine nature (deificatio)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctifying grace effects a real, though accidental and analogical, participation of the soul in the divine nature: 'to be made partakers of the divine nature' (2 Pet. I, 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The participation is not literal deification of substance (avoids pantheism), nor merely an external/moral resemblance; instead it is an assimilation or transfiguration that imparts truly supernatural gifts proper to God (e.g., beatific vision ultimately). Theological nuance: which divine attributes are communicated is debated—some emphasize holiness/spirituality and intellectual participation in God's absolute intellectuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of sanctifying grace: sanctity (formal effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: One principal formal effect of sanctifying grace is sanctity—removal of sin and establishment of holiness, making the justified person a living member of Christ's mystical body and granting peace of conscience and special providential assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited Tridentine language: justification is 'not remission of sins merely, but also the sanctification and renewal of the inward man.' Practical fruits: hatred of mortal sin, progress in virtue, peace, strengthened resistance to temptation, and divine assistance toward preserving the state of grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of sanctifying grace: supernatural beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctifying grace beautifies the soul—described by Fathers as a 'splendid painting', 'statue of gold', 'shining light', and by the Roman Catechism as 'a certain splendor and light that effaces all the stains of our souls.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This effect is treated as certain from Revelation and Patristic testimony even if not formalized in a strict ecclesiastical definition; used pastorally and devotionally to illustrate inward transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification consists in infusion of sanctifying grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Justification, properly understood under Catholic doctrine and Trent's teaching, consists in the infusion of sanctifying grace, effecting remission of sins and interior sanctification, not merely an external imputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by Scripture, Tradition, and the Fathers; pre-Tridentine debates (some theologians thought of actual graces only) were rejected as incompatible with Trent. Infant baptism's effects used as an argument for infusion rather than a series of discrete acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments from common sense against the imputation theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical/common-sense objections to Protestant 'imputation' of Christ's righteousness: (1) would imply all Christians have exactly the same degree of sanctity; (2) justification obtained by fiduciary faith could not be lost except by the sin of unbelief; (3) would imply infants cannot be justified by baptism because they cannot apprehend external righteousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These consequences are presented as absurd or morally destructive (the second leading to immoral exhortations attributed to Luther) and historically contributed to the rejection of infant baptism by some sects; used rhetorically to bolster Catholic doctrine of infused sanctifying grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical taxonomy applied to grace (entitative vs operative habit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theologians apply Scholastic categories: grace is primarily an entitative habit (a quality inhering in the soul's substance) though it also has operative aspects (conferring power to perform supernatural acts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why traditional philosophical language is strained: Aristotle's taxonomy lacks a perfect slot for a supernatural infused quality that is not a pure operative habit. This taxonomy underpins debates about identity with charity, the method of infusion, and the metaphysical explanation of sanctification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tridentine and patristic support as normative criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Theological positions are weighed against the teaching of the Fathers and the declarations of the Council of Trent—the text repeatedly uses conciliar and patristic authority as the standard for correct doctrinal formulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers are instructed to prefer formulations consistent with Trent and the Fathers (e.g., infusion, inherent charity, permanence) and to view contrary scholastic speculations (that contradict Trent's decree) as no longer tenable.
